settings.title: They pick at dinner, then want snacks an hour later
settings.alt: A boy pushes peas around a full dinner plate while his mum watches
settings.text:
Some pickiness is normal. But when a child who used to eat well starts pushing food around the plate, then raids the pantry an hour later, it’s often a sign their tummy just isn’t feeling settled.

A comfortable gut and a healthy appetite go hand in hand. When digestion feels off, kids don’t feel like eating, and dinner turns into a nightly negotiation.*

settings.title: “My tummy hurts” on school mornings
settings.alt: A mum zips up her son’s jacket at the front door before school
settings.text:
Occasional tummy aches are one of the most common things kids complain about, and they love to show up right when you’re trying to get out the door.

Gas, bloating and an irregular routine can all leave a little tummy uncomfortable. Gentle, time-tested herbs like fennel, anise and licorice have been used for generations to help soothe occasional tummy upsets.*

settings.title: Calmer mornings, no pill battles
settings.quote: The liquid format saved us. My son refuses pills, but this mixes into his morning orange juice and he drinks it without a fuss.
settings.author: Lisa K.

settings.title: A weekend of sweets throws everything off
settings.alt: Two kids and a dog at a picnic with snacks and juice
settings.text:
Birthday parties, holidays, Halloween, the school bake sale. A run of sugar and processed snacks can leave a child’s tummy feeling out of sorts for days afterwards.

You can’t (and shouldn’t) ban every treat. What you can do is give their digestion a little support to get back to its normal rhythm afterwards.*

settings.title: Bathroom trips are all over the place
settings.alt: A mum and daughter reading together on the sofa
settings.text:
Regularity is one of the clearest windows into how a child’s tummy is doing. A few days of nothing, then the opposite, usually means their digestion isn’t in a steady rhythm.

Traditional botanicals like black walnut and clove have long been used to support the body’s natural digestive rhythm and regularity.*

settings.title: They touch everything (and everything ends up in their mouth)
settings.alt: A boy playing in a park sandpit
settings.text:
Sandpits, playgrounds, pets, shared crayons, the classroom. Kids are little explorers, and that’s a good thing. It just means their tummies are busy every single day, especially in school season.

Herbs like pau d’arco, thyme and oregano are traditionally used to support healthy gut defences through busy school terms.*

settings.title: A quick, honest word on worms
settings.text:
You may have seen parents online talking about parasite cleanses for kids. Here’s the honest version: pinworms are very common in school-age children. If your child has an itchy bottom (especially at night) or you spot tiny white threads, see your doctor. It’s quick and easy to treat with the right medicine.

ParaPatrol isn’t a worm treatment and doesn’t replace your doctor. It’s a gentle daily herbal routine for the everyday stuff: tummy comfort, digestion and appetite.*

settings.alt: ParaPatrol with fennel, anise, licorice root and aloe vera
settings.text:
Adult tinctures are dosed for grown-ups and are often made with alcohol. Pills turn into a battle. And anything that tastes “healthy” gets pushed straight back across the table.
